Here are two facts that changed how I think about small experiments.

The first is that how you split the sample into control and treatment groups
matters. Consider an experiment with 400 pupils, where the aim is to test
whether an intervention improves test scores. If you pair up pupils with similar
test scores before the experiment, then randomly assign control/treatment within
each pair, the results will be as precise as one run on 1,200 pupils where the
pupils are split at random and analysed with a two-sample t-test.

The second is how you analyse the results matters. In the example above, if you
analysed the data from the paired experiment design with a two-sample t-test
instead of a paired t-test, the gain from the design would be lost. The
precision comes from the pairs, and an ordinary two-sample test cannot see them,
so it reports an interval too wide and misses effects it should have caught.

This site goes through some techniques for improving the design of small
experiments, and explains how to analyse them correctly. **Pairwise matching**
splits the sample into pairs that are as alike as possible and randomly assigns
control/treatment within each pair. **Rerandomization** draws multiple ordinary
random splits, scores each on how balanced it is, and keeps the most balanced
one. **The Mahalanobis distance** is the distance metric both of them use to
decide how alike two units are.

All the code is Python, is available at
[this repository](https://github.com/AlexanderDBolton/BoostSampleSize).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
